description: First real run of the user's dedicated binary none-vs-not-none classifier (script committed directly by the user at 317559a, not built by this session), pivoting away from the LoRA-generative-Qwen track per explicit user request ('try using smaller, simpler models like encoders + MLPs'). LoRA-adapted roberta-base (r=8/alpha=16, query/value target modules), --context full, --class-weight (inverse-train-freq CE weighting) + --oversample-none 3, epochs=5, batch-size=16, max-length=512, test-holdout=500 (split_seed=random, fresh). MUCH cheaper than the Qwen generative track: ~45s/epoch (vs 13-17min/epoch for Qwen3-0.6B at max-length 4096) and only ~1-5GB VRAM (vs ~16-18GB) -- roberta-base is 125M params vs Qwen3-0.6B's 600M, and only the classifier head + LoRA adapters + query/value projections train (889K trainable params, 0.7%). RESULT: dev macro_f1=0.759 (none_precision=1.000/recall=0.357/f1=0.526, i.e. every none-prediction was correct but the model was conservative, missing 9/14 gold none) vs test macro_f1=0.611 (none_precision=0.250/recall=0.222/f1=0.235, tp=2/fp=6/fn=7 on 9 gold none in this holdout draw) -- a real generalization gap (-0.148 macro), similar magnitude of dev/test disagreement to what the Qwen generative track saw on its first (non-replicated) pos-weight+oversample attempt. Best epoch plateaued at epoch 3 (macro_f1=0.759, unchanged through epoch 5) -- train loss kept dropping (0.64->0.21) without further dev gains, a mild overfitting signal past epoch 3. CONCLUSION: a real, working, MUCH cheaper alternative to the generative approach for isolating the none class, but not yet clearly better at generalizing -- test none_f1 (0.235) is in a similar range to the generative track's early attempts (before pos-weight+oversample replication settled around 0.375-0.500 test none F1). Worth a replicate (fresh split) before drawing firm conclusions, same lesson as the generative track's rotating-test-holdout noise floor. Next: the full 5-way st1 classifier (lora_train_st1_classifier.py, new script this session).

First run of a NEW script (lora_train_st1_classifier.py, written this session, generalizing the user's binary lora_train_st1_none.py to the full 5-way st1 taxonomy: digital_content_or_services/none/other/physical_goods/physical_services). Same encoder+MLP philosophy as the binary run above -- LoRA-adapted roberta-base (r=8/alpha=16, query/value), --context full, --class-weight (inverse-train-freq per-class CE weighting) + --oversample-rare-st1 3 (duplicates none/other, the two classes under 5%% train freq), epochs=5, batch-size=16, max-length=512, test-holdout=500 fresh split. Smoke-tested end to end (--sample-size 16 --epochs 1 --device cpu) before this real run. RESULT: dev macro_f1=0.598 (best at epoch 5; per-label: digital=0.876, none=0.452, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.872, physical_services=0.792), test macro_f1=0.559 (digital=0.897, none=0.381, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.862, physical_services=0.654) -- dev and test AGREE closely (gap -0.039) and dev>=test, the trustworthy generalization pattern per updated feedback_rotating_test_holdout guidance. Does NOT collapse: unlike an unweighted/no-oversample baseline would likely do (untested here, but matches the generative track's own baseline-vs-lever story), none gets real, non-trivial F1 on both dev (0.452) and test (0.381), broadly comparable to (and on test, only slightly below) the binary none-only classifier's dev=0.526/test=0.235 -- the joint 5-way task's none score is actually MORE stable/higher on test than the binary-only model's, plausibly because the 5-way softmax's class-weighted CE spreads useful signal across all classes at once rather than optimizing a single binary boundary in isolation. 'other' stayed at 0.000 both dev/test (near-zero train instances, consistent with every other 'other'-label finding across both the encoder and generative tracks this session -- essentially unlearnable at this data scale regardless of architecture). Training is dramatically cheaper than the Qwen3-0.6B generative track: full 5-epoch run (train+dev eval every epoch+test-holdout) completed in ~4.5 minutes wall-clock (vs 60-90+ minutes for the generative track's 5-epoch runs), ~1-5GB VRAM vs ~16-18GB. CONCLUSION: a genuinely working, much cheaper 'just st1' encoder+MLP classifier that does not collapse on the rare classes, with the best dev/test agreement seen in this session across BOTH tracks (generative and encoder) -- strong candidate to replicate (fresh split) and potentially extend (legal-bert-base as an alternate encoder, deeper unfrozen-layer counts, or last_layer_train.py's frozen-encoder variant for an even cheaper baseline).

REPLICATE (fresh split) of the binary none-vs-not classifier. Striking result: dev metrics are an EXACT match to the first run (macro_f1=0.759, none precision=1.000/recall=0.357/f1=0.526, identical tp=5/fp=0/fn=9 counts) despite a different train/test-holdout split -- dev.jsonl is fixed and unaffected by the split, and the model's decision behavior on it converged identically both times, a good sign of low training variance for this small/cheap setup. Test differs from the first run as expected (rotating holdout, different composition): macro_f1=0.663 (vs first run's 0.611, +0.052), none_f1=0.333 (vs 0.235, tp=2/fp=1/fn=7 this time vs tp=2/fp=6/fn=7) -- same general ballpark, consistent direction (dev>=test both times), no contradiction. CONCLUSION: dev result for this model/recipe is highly reproducible; test still carries meaningful noise from small none gold counts in the rotating holdout, same lesson as the generative track, but nothing here contradicts the first run's read.

REPLICATE (fresh split) of the 5-way st1 classifier. RESULT: dev macro_f1=0.559 (vs first run's 0.598, -0.039), test macro_f1=0.553 (vs first run's 0.559, -0.006) -- both runs land in a similar band (0.55-0.60 dev, 0.55-0.56 test) and BOTH replicates show the same excellent dev/test agreement pattern (gap -0.006 here vs -0.039 in the first run, both dev>=test). none F1: dev=0.370 (vs first run's 0.452), test=0.286 (vs first run's 0.381) -- somewhat lower this time but still clearly non-zero/non-collapsed on both dev and test, and 'other' again stayed at 0.000 both runs. CONCLUSION: the 5-way encoder+MLP classifier reproduces its core finding cleanly across two independent splits -- real, working, non-collapsing st1 classification with consistently strong dev/test agreement (the best-agreeing config found anywhere in this session, both generative and encoder tracks), at a small fraction of the generative track's compute cost. This is now the most trustworthy 'just st1' result of the session.

Alternate-encoder comparison: same recipe as the roberta-base 5-way runs (r=8/alpha=16 LoRA on query/value, --context full, --class-weight + --oversample-rare-st1 3, epochs=5, batch-size=16, lr=2e-4, untuned -- no LR retune attempted for this different base model), swapping FacebookAI/roberta-base for nlpaueb/legal-bert-base-uncased (already fully cached locally, 841MB, confirmed not an empty stub before running). RESULT: clearly worse and slower-converging than roberta-base at identical hyperparameters. Train loss barely moved through epoch 3 (1.48->1.29, vs roberta's 1.39->0.60) and even by epoch 5 was still at 0.96 (roberta plateaus near 0.4-0.5 by epoch 2-3). Dev macro_f1 only reached 0.394 by epoch 5 (still climbing, no plateau reached -- vs roberta's ~0.55-0.60 plateau by epoch 2-3), and worse, TEST none F1 collapsed to 0.000 (vs roberta's 0.286-0.381 on both replicates) despite dev showing some none signal (0.140-0.186) -- a real generalization failure on the weakest class, not just slower convergence. CONCLUSION: legal-bert-base-uncased is a clearly worse fit for this task at these (roberta-tuned) hyperparameters -- plausibly its legal-domain pretraining vocabulary/style is a poor match for informal video-transcript/livestream content, or it simply needs a different (likely higher) LR / more epochs to reach comparable performance -- NOT tuned here, this is an apples-to-apples-hyperparameters comparison only. Discarding for now; would need its own LR sweep before writing off the architecture entirely, but roberta-base remains the clear standing choice for this encoder track.

Hyperparameter sweep on the 5-way st1 classifier (HANDOFF next-candidate #2), fresh split, capacity bump vs the r8/a16 baseline: --lora-r 16 --lora-alpha 32, everything else unchanged (--class-weight --oversample-rare-st1 3, single LR=2e-4 for both LoRA and head, epochs=5, test-holdout=500). Best dev checkpoint was epoch 3 (macro_f1=0.586, per-label: digital=0.880, none=0.400, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.873, physical_services=0.776) -- dev plateaued/slightly regressed epoch 4-5 (0.582 both), same pattern as the baseline's epoch-3 plateau. Test macro_f1=0.537 (digital=0.883, none=0.261, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.865, physical_services=0.679), dev/test gap -0.049 (dev>=test, still the trustworthy direction) but both dev and especially test none_f1 (0.261) land BELOW the r8/a16 baseline's two replicates (dev 0.452/0.370, test 0.381/0.286) and below the r16a32 capacity bump's own dev (0.400). CONCLUSION: capacity bump does not help this task, consistent with Track 1's own r16a32-regresses-at-r32 finding (inverted-U) -- here the regression shows up even at r16, one step earlier than Track 1's sweep. r8/a16 remains the standing default; no reason to move up in capacity for this classifier.

Hyperparameter sweep on the 5-way st1 classifier (HANDOFF next-candidate #2), fresh split, separate higher head LR vs the r8/a16 single-LR baseline: --head-lr 1e-3 (LoRA adapters stay at --lr 2e-4), everything else unchanged. Best dev checkpoint was epoch 4 (macro_f1=0.587, per-label: digital=0.889, none=0.519, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.862, physical_services=0.667) -- notably dev none_f1=0.519 is the BEST none score seen anywhere in this classifier's history (vs baseline's 0.370-0.452), suggesting the faster-learning head does help the rare class ON DEV. But test macro_f1=0.547 (digital=0.892, none=0.200, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.879, physical_services=0.765) and test none_f1 COLLAPSED to 0.200, the worst test none score seen for this classifier and a much larger dev-test gap on the none label specifically (0.519->0.200) than the baseline ever showed -- a real generalization failure on the one class this change was meant to help, not just noise (the overall macro gap, -0.040, still looks fine and hides this). CONCLUSION: separate head-LR=1e-3 overfits the none class to the dev split specifically; do NOT adopt over the single-LR r8/a16 baseline. Neither sweep direction (capacity or head-LR) beat the standing default this round -- r8/a16/single-LR/oversample-rare-st1=3 remains the best config found for this classifier.

Hyperparameter sweep on the 5-way st1 classifier (untried axis flagged in HANDOFF), fresh split, oversample factor DOWN vs the standing --oversample-rare-st1 3: --oversample-rare-st1 2, everything else unchanged (r8/a16, --class-weight, single LR=2e-4, epochs=5, test-holdout=500). Best dev checkpoint epoch 3 (macro_f1=0.580, per-label: digital=0.873, none=0.500, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.872, physical_services=0.656) -- note dev none_f1=0.500 is the 2nd-best dev none score seen for this classifier (behind only the head-lr=1e-3 run's 0.519, which collapsed on test). Test macro_f1=0.568 (digital=0.877, none=0.400, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.879, physical_services=0.684) -- BEATS both oversample=3 baseline replicates on test macro_f1 (0.559/0.553) AND test none_f1 (0.400 vs 0.381/0.286), with the tightest dev/test gap seen for this classifier (0.012, vs baseline's 0.039/0.006). CONCLUSION: lighter oversampling (2x instead of 3x) looks like a genuine improvement, not just noise -- less aggressive duplication of the rare none/other class may reduce a mild overfit-to-duplicates effect while still giving the class-weighted loss enough rare-class exposure. Promising candidate for PRIMARY standing default; needs a fresh-split replicate before promoting over oversample=3, per standing practice (every surprising result this session has required replication before trusting it).

Hyperparameter sweep on the 5-way st1 classifier, fresh split, oversample factor UP vs the standing --oversample-rare-st1 3: --oversample-rare-st1 5, everything else unchanged. Best dev checkpoint epoch 3 (macro_f1=0.553, per-label: digital=0.859, none=0.364, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.861, physical_services=0.680). Test macro_f1=0.525 (digital=0.868, none=0.296, other=0.000, physical_goods=0.848, physical_services=0.615), dev/test gap 0.028 (dev>=test, agrees) but both dev and test macro/none land below the oversample=3 baseline's two replicates. CONCLUSION: heavier oversampling regresses, consistent with the oversample=2 result above -- more train-set duplication of the rare classes appears to hurt rather than help this classifier, opposite of what the generative track found (Track 1 uses oversample=3 as part of its own winning recipe, but that track's rare-class base rate and duplication mechanics differ). Combined with the oversample=2 finding, the emerging pattern is: LESS oversampling of rare st1 labels is better for this encoder+MLP classifier. Discarding =5; oversample=2 is now the leading candidate to replicate next.

REPLICATE (fresh split) of --oversample-rare-st1 2. Dev macro_f1=0.574 (best@epoch5, none=0.368) is close to run 1's dev=0.580 -- reproduces fine. But test macro_f1=0.532 (vs run1's 0.568) and test none_f1=0.160 (vs run1's 0.400!) -- a large swing on the none label specifically between the two fresh-split draws, the same rotating-test-holdout noise pattern flagged in feedback_rotating_test_holdout (small none gold counts per draw). CORRECTION to the optimistic read after run 1: oversample=2's test macro_f1 across both replicates (0.568, 0.532, mean~0.550) lands in essentially the SAME band as the oversample=3 baseline's two replicates (0.559, 0.553, mean~0.556) -- not a confirmed improvement, the first run's apparent win was likely a favorable draw on which none instances fell in the holdout, not a real effect of the lighter oversampling factor. CONCLUSION: oversample=2 is NOT clearly better than oversample=3; both are roughly equivalent on this noisy small-none-count metric. Do not promote oversample=2 over the standing oversample=3 default -- treat as inconclusive, filed under 'keep' only because it's a valid data point, not because it won.

NEW LEVER: --undersample-majority-st1 (added this round, complementary to --oversample-rare-st1 -- randomly drops train instances of majority-frequency st1 labels down to 1/factor of their original count instead of duplicating rare ones). Solo test, factor=2 (halve digital_content_or_services and physical_goods), --class-weight kept, --oversample-rare-st1 left at default 1 (off). Best dev checkpoint epoch5 (macro_f1=0.574, none=0.378). Test macro_f1=0.476, test none_f1=0.214 -- clearly BELOW the plain oversample=3 baseline's two replicates (test 0.559/0.553, test none 0.381/0.286) on every metric. CONCLUSION: shrinking majority-class training data hurts more than class-weighting+selective rare-oversampling helps -- the majority classes still count equally toward macro F1, so starving them of real training signal is a net loss even though it nominally rebalances the label ratio.

Solo undersample-majority test, factor=3 (keep 1/3 of digital_content_or_services and physical_goods), same setup as factor=2 above. Best dev checkpoint epoch5 (macro_f1=0.518, none=0.316) -- notably worse than factor=2's dev=0.574, and the epoch curve is much noisier/slower to converge (epoch1 macro_f1=0.147 vs factor=2's 0.137, but epoch2=0.332 vs 0.537 -- less data per epoch clearly slows learning). Test macro_f1=0.521 (higher than factor=2's 0.476, but still below baseline's 0.553-0.559), test none_f1=0.222. CONCLUSION: heavier undersampling (factor=3) is worse on dev, roughly a wash with factor=2 on test (both still below baseline) -- confirms the direction (undersampling majority classes is a net negative for this classifier), consistent with the factor=2 result. Neither undersample factor is competitive with the standing oversample-only default.

COMBINED-LEVER + ORDER ABLATION (undersample-first arm): --undersample-majority-st1 2 + --oversample-rare-st1 3 together, applying undersample_majority() BEFORE oversample_rare() (this script's default order when both are set -- undersample computed on original distribution, then oversample computed on the already-shrunk set). Run by a peer Claude Code session coordinating on this same repo/branch (same standing r8/a16/class-weight/full-context/test-holdout=500 recipe). Best dev checkpoint epoch3 (macro_f1=0.542, none=0.340). Test macro_f1=0.474, test none_f1=0.190 -- below the oversample-only baseline (0.553-0.559/0.286-0.381) and in the same regressed band as the solo undersample runs above. Paired with the oversample-first arm below for a clean order ablation (same factors, same split... different fresh splits actually, see caveat in that row).

COMBINED-LEVER + ORDER ABLATION (oversample-first arm): same --undersample-majority-st1 2 + --oversample-rare-st1 3, but with a NEW --oversample-first flag (added this round) reversing the order -- oversample_rare() runs first (on the original distribution, tripling none/other), THEN undersample_majority() runs on that already-oversampled set. Interaction effect confirmed in the logs: after oversampling, 'none' crosses the 5%% majority threshold and gets swept into the undersample step too, partially undoing its own oversampling (train ends at 958 instances vs the undersample-first arm's 998 -- fewer, despite nominally 'more' manipulation). Best dev checkpoint epoch4 (macro_f1=0.567, none=0.400). Test macro_f1=0.515, test none_f1=0.143. VS the undersample-first arm (dev=0.542/test=0.474, on a different fresh split -- not a perfectly controlled comparison, same rotating-test-holdout caveat as always): oversample-first wins on macro F1 both dev (+0.025) and test (+0.041), but LOSES on test none_f1 (0.143 vs 0.190) -- the macro gain comes from the majority classes recovering some ground, not from oversample-first helping the rare class it was nominally applied to first. CONCLUSION: order of combining these two levers has a real, mechanistic effect (confirmed via the threshold-crossing interaction, not just noise) but NEITHER order is competitive with the oversample-only baseline (test macro_f1 0.553-0.559) -- undersampling majority classes remains a net negative in this classifier regardless of when it's applied relative to oversampling. Standing default (--class-weight --oversample-rare-st1 3, no undersampling) is unchanged and remains the best config found.

NEW LEVER, discovered via investigation (not user-requested this round -- autonomous follow-up): roberta-base's 512-token position-embedding ceiling means --context full at --max-length 512 silently truncates away the product PAGE block for most instances under HF's default right-truncation (keep start/drop end), since render_context puts TRANSCRIPT first and PAGE last. Measured: PAGE block starts after token 512 (i.e. is ENTIRELY dropped) in 234/300 (78%) of a random train sample; median full_context length is 1268 tokens vs the 512 budget. This silently undermines the --context full flag's intent for the entire encoder+MLP track -- Track 1 (generative Qwen, max-length 4096) genuinely sees the full context and confirmed it matters (feedback_st1_focus.md), but Track 2 has been running something much closer to transcript-only for most instances without anyone noticing. Added --truncation-side {left,right} flag (sets tokenizer.truncation_side before building datasets); 'left' keeps the END of the rendered text instead, preserving PAGE content at the cost of the transcript's tail. RESULT (paired same-session comparison, fresh splits, standing r8/a16/class-weight/oversample=3 recipe otherwise identical): truncation-side=left dev macro_f1=0.622 (best@epoch5, none=0.500) vs right's dev=0.543 (none=0.276) -- +0.079 macro, +0.224 none. Test: left macro_f1=0.546/none_f1=0.316 vs right's macro_f1=0.491/none_f1=0.190 -- +0.055 macro, +0.126 none. Both dev>=test (trustworthy direction), left's dev=0.622 is the best dev score seen anywhere in this classifier's history (previous best 0.598). CONCLUSION: strong, mechanistically-explained lead -- preserving the product-page content that Track 1 already confirmed matters for st1, instead of silently dropping it to truncation, looks like a genuine architecture-level fix rather than a hyperparameter nudge. NOT yet replicated -- launching a fresh-split replicate before promoting to standing default, per standing practice (every surprising result this session needed replication).

REPLICATE (fresh split) of --truncation-side left. Dev macro_f1=0.645 (best@epoch5, none=0.562) -- even higher than run 1's 0.622, confirming the effect is real and not a lucky draw; both runs' dev score (0.622, 0.645) clearly clear every other config tried in this classifier's entire history (previous best 0.598). Test macro_f1=0.538 (vs run1's 0.546, close), test none_f1=0.222 (vs run1's 0.316, some spread -- consistent with the known small-none-count test-holdout noise pattern, not a contradiction). Both replicates show strong dev>=test agreement (gaps 0.076 and 0.107). CONCLUSION: --truncation-side left REPLICATES CLEANLY and is PROMOTED to the new standing default for lora_train_st1_classifier.py, superseding the implicit right-truncation default used by every prior run this session. Mechanistic explanation (preserving the product-PAGE content that Track 1 independently confirmed is decisive for st1, instead of silently truncating it away) makes this a trustworthy, non-coincidental finding, not just a hyperparameter nudge. New standing config: --model FacebookAI/roberta-base --context full --max-length 512 --truncation-side left --lora-r 8 --lora-alpha 16 --target-modules query,value --class-weight --oversample-rare-st1 3.

Re-test of the previously-discarded capacity bump (--lora-r 16 --lora-alpha 32) under the NEW --truncation-side left baseline, to check whether the earlier regression was an artifact of the truncated (page-less) context rather than a real capacity effect. Best dev checkpoint epoch5 (macro_f1=0.630, none=0.516) -- within the new baseline's dev range (0.622-0.645) but at its low end. Test macro_f1=0.516 (below baseline's 0.538-0.546) and test none_f1=0.000 (a collapse, despite dev none=0.516 looking fine) -- a real generalization failure on the rare class. CONCLUSION: capacity bump STILL underperforms r8/a16 even with the truncation fix -- the inverted-U capacity finding is independent of the truncation issue, not an artifact of it. r8/a16 remains standing.

Re-test of --oversample-rare-st1 2 (previously inconclusive/didn't replicate) under the NEW --truncation-side left baseline. Best dev checkpoint epoch5 (macro_f1=0.612, none=0.444) -- below the new oversample=3 baseline's dev range (0.622-0.645). Test macro_f1=0.541 (right in the baseline's 0.538-0.546 band, essentially a match) but test none_f1=0.182 (below baseline's 0.222-0.316). CONCLUSION: oversample=2 is roughly on par with oversample=3 on test macro but not better, and worse on dev and none -- confirms oversample=3 remains the right choice, the earlier inconclusive read (before the truncation fix) wasn't hiding a real effect that only shows up with more context. Oversample factor is a fully closed question now.

Follow-up to the truncation-side fix: diagnostic showed even --truncation-side left still loses PAGE's own START (product title/category, plausibly the most informative part) for 42%% of instances when PAGE alone exceeds the remaining 510-token budget. Built --page-token-budget N (new flag + ST1Dataset._encode_budgeted): reserves N tokens for PAGE specifically (kept from PAGE's start, tokenized/sliced independently) and gives the rest of the 510-token budget to the transcript+metadata prefix (kept from the prefix's end, closest to PAGE) -- guarantees both segments always get a fixed slice regardless of instance length, unlike whole-string truncation which is all-or-nothing per instance. Verified correctness via a standalone decode check (confirmed PAGE-like content -- prices, product names, payment methods -- appears at the sequence tail as intended) before running. RESULT at budget=300: dev macro_f1=0.578 (best@epoch3, none=0.341), test macro_f1=0.560/none_f1=0.300. Below the plain truncation-side=left baseline's dev range (0.622-0.645) though slightly above its test range (0.538-0.546). CONCLUSION: the fixed budget split does NOT clearly beat plain left-truncation -- likely because it forces prefix truncation on every instance regardless of need, whereas whole-string left-truncation only truncates when the instance actually exceeds 512 tokens (many don't). Test edge is within this task's established noise band, dev (the cleaner signal) is worse. Discarding budget=300 relative to the simpler, already-confirmed truncation-side=left default.

Same --page-token-budget mechanism as above, budget=400 (more room for PAGE, less for prefix). Best dev epoch4 (macro_f1=0.616, none=0.444) -- closer to the plain truncation-side=left baseline's dev range (0.622-0.645) than budget=300 was, but still at/below its low end, with a notably noisier early-epoch convergence (epoch1 macro_f1=0.294, a big dip vs plain left-truncation's smoother epoch1=~0.45-0.50). Test macro_f1=0.558/none_f1=0.364 -- again slightly above the plain baseline's test range, same pattern as budget=300. CONCLUSION: increasing the page budget from 300->400 moves dev closer to (but not past) the plain-truncation baseline -- consistent with the hypothesis that the fixed-split mechanism is strictly worse than adaptive whole-string truncation for instances that don't need PAGE-specific budgeting, and the gain from including PAGE's very start (vs whatever partial PAGE tail plain left-truncation would keep) isn't enough to offset that cost. NOT pursuing further budget values -- the direction is clear enough (added complexity without a confirmed win). Standing default remains plain --truncation-side left (no --page-token-budget).

Max-length sweep (user asked to characterize how much context window is worth, before swapping in a longer-context model): --max-length 128 with --truncation-side left, everything else standing (r8/a16/class-weight/oversample=3). At this tiny budget, left-truncation keeps only the last 128 tokens -- almost entirely a tail slice of PAGE content (price/product-name lines), essentially zero transcript signal for most instances. Best dev epoch4 (macro_f1=0.616, none=0.541). Test macro_f1=0.577/none_f1=0.519 -- both the BEST test scores seen anywhere in this classifier's history, surprisingly. CONCLUSION: informative but likely partly noise given small test-holdout none counts (same caveat as everywhere else this session) -- but notable that even a minimal PAGE-tail slice carries strong signal, consistent with the truncation-side finding's premise that PAGE content matters a lot for st1. Not conclusively 'better than 512' given the established noise band, but a useful data point for the context-length-vs-performance curve.

Same sweep, --max-length 256. Best dev epoch5 (macro_f1=0.595, none=0.437), test macro_f1=0.509/none_f1=0.222 -- worse than both 128 and 512 on test, non-monotonic with respect to length. CONCLUSION: the max-length-vs-performance relationship in the 128-512 range is noisy/non-monotonic on this small test-holdout, not a clean trend -- don't over-read a single sweep point. Filed as a data point for the context-length curve, not as a standalone recommendation.

Re-test of legal-bert-base-uncased with TWO fixes applied vs the original untuned attempt: --truncation-side left (this session's major finding) and a higher LR (5e-4 vs the original 2e-4, borrowed straight from roberta's tuned recipe -- per the original attempt's conclusion that legal-bert 'would need its own LR sweep before writing off the architecture').
